title: Musicians in Bending Towards the Light: Doc Cheatham and Ron Carter
summary: Early casts, Doc Cheatham's misunderstanding, and Ron Carter's magical guest bass appearance.

blocks.x: In Utica here, we did it.
Oh that’s right. You’re in Utica.
Yes I saw it, you probably were there.
It’s a wonderful production. I’m guessing that you have significant powers of persuasion.
Yes right. There is a limit to that. But I envision the whole idea and then approaching these musicians and you did well.

Well it’s very funny because that first year nobody knew what it was you know. I mean I got — the very first year I did it I had Grady Tate, Tommy Flanagan, George Mraz — but a good band and so forth. And they all did it. The second year there’s a whole story in between that that you don’t want to hear. Nevertheless the second year I remember calling Doc Cheatham was a — one of the three kings. Now all I had money for was to rehearse in the afternoon. I had a band rehearsal before and then the day of the show we run the show and then do the show. So it was like 3:00 in the afternoon and we were supposed to be running the show. And — what’s his name —

Wasn’t there. And I called him up and he said, “Oh I’m just having my lunch.” He said “you know I’m going to play a couple of Christmas songs, right?” I said, “No.” Because he had no concept of this being a show and it’s quite different when you’re working with musicians and you want them to come forward here and, you know. But we have a director now, Beth Ann Kennedy, who really can connect. The first couple of directors didn’t really connect with the musicians as well. But they love it now and, you know, I had this year, in New York I had Ron Carter. And Ron as a special guest. Now he played it in the very second show and he never forgot it. Because every time I’d see him somewhere he’d say, “Oh that was so great” and so forth. But I hadn’t had him in the band since. But this time I decided to ask him to be a special guest, which is after the whole play itself and then it goes into the celebration of “Deck the Halls” when all these different people come out and play. And that’s where I was going to put him. And he said, “Well who’s your bass player?” I said, “Dean Johnson.” He said, “Can I use his bass?” And I said, “Yeah, I’ll call him, I don’t think he’ll have a problem with that.” And I will tell you, it was utter magic. Because it was during the finale, it was right after the tap dancers so it was all this — it was big. And then absolute silence and he went down and Dean handed him his bass, and there was wood floors for one thing. The sound was extraordinary. And utter silence from the audience, because they really couldn’t believe © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

who they were seeing and hearing. And it was just gorgeous. And the next day I got a call from him, he said, “What’s your address I want to send you something.” And in it was his book that’s the Smithsonian interviews. It’s a gorgeous book, color and so forth. With a good add: To Anne, thank you, Ron. He’s thanking me. So that’s how much the musicians love it.

It’s interesting you said that about sort of corralling the musicians and said, “Okay after this number then you have to go over here.” And I had that experience doing a show with a singer, a Billie Holiday show, and you know she would say, “After this thing you say this and then I’ll say this.” And I was going, “What do you mean?” It’s theater.
Yes. We could never get Phil Woods to come forward enough. We let him wear his hat as a crown but —
